Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. - **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Let me read the issue.

{"number":1030,"title":"sheepdog: the FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN permission list is spelled seven times, and only RULES.md has all of it","body":"## What happened

`missingbulb/Shepherd` adopted `sheepdog` with a PAT granted Metadata read, Contents read/write, Issues read/write, Actions read/write — **no Pull requests: Read**. Four sweeps ran green on it for two days. `fleet-digest` did not: its collector walks each member's closed pull requests, and a fine-grained PAT reads a *public* repo's pull requests without that permission but a *private* one's not at all. The first private member in the walk answered `403`, prework threw, and because the failed work item stays open the queue filed no item behind it — the task stopped being scheduled, not merely failing. Two days of briefs missing before anyone looked. (Shepherd [#37](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/37), [#3](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/3).)

## The gap

The required permission set is written out in seven places, and each is the subset its own author needed:

| where | what it says |
|---|---|
| `packs/sheepdog/RULES.md` | Metadata, Contents r/w, Issues r/w, **Pull requests read**, Actions r/w — the only complete one |
| `tasks/fleet-roster/check-fleet-roster.mjs` | Metadata, Contents read, Issues r/w |
| `tasks/fleet-pack-seeds/check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs` | Metadata, Contents **r/w**, Issues r/w |
| `tasks/fleet-baseline/force-fleet-baseline.mjs` | Metadata, Contents read, Actions r/w |
| `tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/worker.mjs` | Metadata, Contents read, Issues r/w, Actions r/w |
| `tasks/fleet-usage/aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs` | Metadata, Contents read |
| `tasks/fleet-digest/worker.mjs` | Metadata, Contents read, **Pull requests read**, Issues read |

Also `tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/task.md:23` — "the one fleet credential is `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` (Contents read, Issues read/write, Actions read+write)", which reads like the whole answer and is not.

A per-task message stating its own task's needs is defensible in isolation. What makes it a bug is that these strings are the *only* machine-readable statement of the requirement — `required_secrets` carries a name and nothing else — so a session writing an adopting repo's human-steps issue assembles the list from them and lands the union of six subsets, missing exactly the one permission no other sweep needs. That is what Shepherd's checklist did.

Two further things make it hard to catch:

- **Nothing validates the grant.** Every one of those strings is emitted only when the secret is *absent*. A token that exists but is short a permission fails deep in a run as a bare `403` with no hint that a permission is the cause.
- **The failure is invisible on a public-only fleet.** The digest only 403s once a member is private, so a fleet can run correctly for months and then break on the day someone adds a private repo.

Fixes #1030.

The permission list was spelled in seven places, each the subset its own author needed. Those strings were the only machine-readable statement of the requirement, so a human assembling a grant out of them landed the union of the subsets and missed `Pull requests: read` — needed only by the digest, and only once a member is private.

## What changed

**`packs/sheepdog/`** — new `fleet-token.mjs`: one table, a row per fine-grained-PAT permission carrying the access to grant, why it is needed, which sweep uses it at what level, and the endpoints it covers. Everything about the token now renders from it:

- every sweep's "token is not set" message names the **whole** grant first, then that sweep's own subset as explanation (`missingFleetTokenError`). The six hand-written strings are gone.
- `pack.mjs` gains `adoptionHandover` built from the table, so the adopting session files a checkbox carrying the complete list — ask 2. It also bumps `version` to 10 so enforcers already on 9 receive this.
- `fleet-api.mjs` attributes a `403` to the permission that would fix it, on `paged`, `readFile`, `fileExists`, `putFile` and `classifyDispatch`. This is the cheaper half of the preflight in ask 3: no extra requests, and it reports on the call that actually failed rather than on a probe that may not resemble it. A path no row claims gets no hint — a wrong guess is worse than none.
- `RULES.md`, `README.md`, the task `task.md`/`task.mjs` comments: the lists are replaced by a pointer at the table. Narrative mentions of a single permission ("dispatching is an Actions write") stay.

**`packs-tests/sheepdog/`** — `fleet-token.test.mjs` drives each of the six sweeps' real `main()` with the secret unset and asserts every permission in the table appears; asserts adoption hands over the complete grant; asserts the `403` attribution; and scans every tracked file in the pack for a permission **list** (two or more name+access pairs within two lines) outside `fleet-token.mjs`. Run against the pre-change content that last test flags all seven sites and nothing after. Two older tests asserted the wording that is now retired and were updated.

## Not done

A preflight probe per permission. It cannot be accurate where it matters: `Pull requests: read` fails only on a **private** member, so a probe against the enforcer's own repo would pass on a grant that later 403s, and a probe against a private member is the same request the sweep is about to make anyway. The 403 attribution gets the diagnosis without the guess. Happy to add one if you want it regardless.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `claudinite-growth` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Dispatchable so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR (whose push/open GitHub never
  # turns into a pull_request run — the recursion guard) can still get this
  # suite started on its branch: baselining's deliver() and any bot-authored
  # PR flow (#432, #565) dispatch it explicitly.
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level
        # (`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs` and so on), so a test at an unlisted depth
        # was silently never run — which is exactly how vendoring/'s two files sat outside
        # CI. `**` removes depth from the question; what remains is the root list, and
        # engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the moment a tracked test lands
        # outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit; adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ (migrations included) + the other top-level canon code;
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs-tests/             every canon pack's tests, mirroring packs/
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        #   docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/ the dispatch design's executable scenarios — the
        #                            simulator lives beside the spec it models, not in
        #                            engine/ (nothing ships it; it tests prose)
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/**/*.test.mjs)
          # Deliberately oversubscribed. node --test defaults to one worker per core
          # minus one, which fits a CPU-bound suite; this one spends most of its wall
          # clock waiting — on git plumbing, spawned workers and converge fixtures — so
          # the cores idle at that default (measured on this tree: 106s wall against
          # 187s of user+sys on 4 cores). Doubling the workers: 106s -> 70s, with 16
          # buying only another 2s.
          node --test --test-concurrency=$(( $(nproc) * 2 )) "${tests[@]}"

    carries, and defaults `owner` structurally to the repo's own owner —

    list would otherwise widen a brief in silence.

    the executor closes an item whose task the repo no longer carries as
